intro: Artur Schnabel plays the first movement of Beethoven’s Piano Sonata No. 30, Op. 109, marked Vivace, ma non troppo — Adagio espressivo. Eight bars of quick, quiet music are followed by a slow passage in the manner of an improvisation, and Beethoven built the whole movement from these two tempos.

sections.label: A · Vivace interrupted by Adagio
sections.mNote: Exchanges between the hands, then wide arpeggios

sections.label: Dev · Quick rising phrases, Tempo I
sections.mNote: Tempo I; the hands exchange rising figures

sections.label: A′ · E major returns
sections.mNote: The opening theme returns in octaves.

sections.label: B′ · Adagio espressivo, C-major arpeggios
sections.mNote: The Adagio returns and covers a wider range of the keyboard.

sections.label: Coda · Tempo primo, quick figures and chords
sections.mNote: Tempo primo; quiet chords interrupt the quick figures.

cues.title: Opening Vivace and first Adagio
cues.text: The hands play quick figures in alternation, softly, in E major. After eight bars Beethoven changes to Adagio espressivo, and broad arpeggios and diminished-seventh chords interrupt the opening tune. The arpeggios cover the whole keyboard.
cues.evidence: Beethoven, Werke, Serie 16 No. 153, Breitkopf & Härtel, printed p. 97, bars 1–15. https://www.lvbeethoven.it/wp-content/uploads/2016/11/Opus109.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Return of Tempo I
cues.text: The Adagio reaches its cadence in B major. At Tempo I the interlocking figures return, now rising in repeated phrases. Accents cut into the legato, and the melody expands into octaves.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel score, printed pp. 98–99; the delayed B-major cadence at bar 15 is discussed at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piano_Sonata_No._30_(Beethoven).
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Return of the opening theme in octaves
cues.text: E major and the opening theme return, with the right hand in octaves. Beethoven soon brings the dynamic back down to piano. The hands are still exchanging their short figures when the next Adagio espressivo begins.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel score, printed p. 99, first two systems: octave return, piano and the approach to Adagio espressivo.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Return of the Adagio
cues.text: The slow arpeggios return in E major, then move to C major. Runs descend from the top of the piano into the bass and rise again. Beethoven extends the ending with a diminuendo, a ritardando and a fermata.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel score, printed pp. 99–100; the move from E to C and back is described by Giovanni Biamonti at https://www.lvbeethoven.org/opus109/.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Coda, from bar 66
cues.text: Tempo primo restores the quick exchanges between the hands. In the coda Beethoven also brings them together in a short passage of quiet chords. The movement ends on a chord of E major, held under the pedal.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel score, printed p. 100, coda from bar 66: chordal passage, final piano E-major chord, pedal and fermata.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Schnabel’s recording, Abbey Road, 1932
cues.text: On 22 March 1932 Schnabel recorded Op. 109 for HMV in Abbey Road’s Studio No. 3. The sonata filled three shellac discs, issued as DB 1822–24.
cues.evidence: Session, studio and catalogue numbers in Colin Clarke’s review of Naxos Historical 8.110763, March 2005: https://musicweb-international.com/classrev/2005/Mar05/Beethoven_schnable9_8110763.htm.

transitions.title: Adagio to Tempo I in B major
transitions.to: Dev · Quick rising phrases, Tempo I
transitions.how: The opening eight bars stop before their B-major cadence is complete. The Adagio extends the cadence across arpeggios until bar 15. Tempo I then restores 2/4 and the quick exchanges between the hands, beginning in B major. The left hand takes the melodic figure and the right hand plays above it.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel score, printed pp. 97–98, bars 8–16. Cadence discussion: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piano_Sonata_No._30_(Beethoven).

transitions.title: Rising octaves lead to E major
transitions.from: Dev · Quick rising phrases, Tempo I
transitions.how: The piano rises through repeated figures under a series of crescendos. At the top of the rise the opening theme returns in E major, doubled in octaves, and the left hand plays below it. The Vivace tempo continues. A piano marking follows soon after, and the hands return to the closer spacing of the opening.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel score, printed pp. 98–99; Gerald Larner describes the first theme returning in E major on the crest of a crescendo. https://geraldlarner.com/work/beethoven-sonata-in-e-major-op-109

transitions.title: The Adagio espressivo returns
transitions.how: The metre changes from 2/4 to 3/4 and the marking to Adagio espressivo. The piano’s chords are spread as arpeggios across both hands. This second Adagio begins in E major. The sharps are then cancelled from the key signature for a passage in C major, with low octaves held beneath the runs.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel score, printed p. 99: returning Adagio, cancelled key signature and C-major passage. https://www.lvbeethoven.it/wp-content/uploads/2016/11/Opus109.pdf

transitions.title: A fermata before Tempo primo
transitions.to: Coda · Tempo primo, quick figures and chords
transitions.how: The Adagio’s runs descend into the bass, then climb to a fermata, with a diminuendo and ritardando marked. At bar 66 Tempo primo restores 2/4 and the quick figures in E major. The right hand starts in a high register and the left hand enters after it.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel score, printed p. 100, first two systems, ending at the Tempo primo of bar 66. https://www.lvbeethoven.it/wp-content/uploads/2016/11/Opus109.pdf

composer.epithet: Composer known for a symphony built from a four-note motif and for the string quartets of his last years.
facts: Neefe in Bonn; Haydn, Albrechtsberger and Salieri in Vienna
Bonn until 1792; Vienna and its surrounding villages for the rest of his life
Nine symphonies · five numbered piano concertos · 32 numbered piano sonatas · 16 string quartets · Fidelio
Described his hearing loss in 1801; used conversation books from 1818

quote.text: I live only in my notes.
quote.source: Beethoven to Franz Gerhard Wegeler, Vienna, 29 June 1801; our translation

composer.background:
In March 1778 Johann van Beethoven advertised a concert in Cologne by his six-year-old son. Ludwig was seven. His father, a singer in the electoral chapel at Bonn, hoped to launch another child prodigy; his grandfather, also Ludwig, had risen from singer to Kapellmeister in the same establishment. The boy was baptised on 17 December 1770, probably the day after his birth. By his teens he was playing the organ for services and the viola in the court orchestra, where he learned operas as a member of the string section.

Christian Gottlob Neefe put Bach’s Well-Tempered Clavier before him and helped him into paid employment. The Breuning household supplied books, friendship and a refuge from Johann’s drinking. After his mother died in 1787, Beethoven increasingly supported his younger brothers. In November 1792 the elector sent him to Vienna to study with Haydn. He was expected to return. French troops occupied Bonn in 1794, and the court that paid him ceased to exist.
